1:
**Sub-item 1 — Accesses all elements in historyList and mathList (no bounds errors)**

Award the point when the response iterates over both lists in a way that would reach every element with a legal index, and an access to each list's elements appears somewhere in the corresponding loop body. The access does not have to be unconditional: if the loop bounds are correct and the `get(i)` call occurs anywhere inside the body — including nested inside an `if` block or as part of a short-circuited expression (e.g., `if (x) { ... mathList.get(j) ... }`) — the item is satisfied; do not speculate about whether the guard might skip elements at runtime. Likewise, do not require the accessed value to be used, and do not penalize an early return so long as the bounds and indices would otherwise support accessing all elements.

Deduct only for the two explicitly listed defects: using array syntax to index an ArrayList (`historyList[i]`) or using an index that is genuinely out of bounds, as well as the baseline failures of accessing only one of the two lists or writing an indexed loop with correct bounds that never accesses any element inside the loop. Other syntactic slips in the access expression — `historyList.length`, `historyList.size`, `get(i)` with an implicit receiver, `historyList.get[i]` — are treated as minor notation errors and do not by themselves cost this point, provided the intent to access each element with a legal index is clear.
2:
**Sub-item 2 — "Calls getStudentID and getAbsences on an element from one of the lists"**

Award the point (no_deduct) whenever the response, somewhere in its executable source, invokes both accessor methods on a `CourseRecord` element drawn from `historyList` or `mathList` — e.g., `hist.getStudentID()` and `math.getAbsences()`. What matters is that the values are actually obtained by invoking the accessors on a record object; the surrounding logic is irrelevant to this item, so a response still earns the point if the comparison logic is wrong (`>=` instead of `>`, `==` on Strings, assuming parallel indices), if it has bounds errors, or if it uses array syntax to reach the ArrayList elements. Reachability does not matter either: a call sitting in a loop that cannot iterate, after an unconditional `return`, or in a branch that is never taken still counts, because the presence of the correct call is sufficient. Be tolerant of surface fidelity when the intent is unmistakable and the call is applied to a `CourseRecord` element — minor case or spelling slips in the method name, a stray argument, or near-miss syntax still count as calling `getStudentID` and `getAbsences`. Likewise, do not apply "ever incorrect" as a global poison: once the response contains at least one correct call to each of the two methods on a `CourseRecord` element from one of the lists, additional stray or malformed invocations elsewhere (in dead code, an unused helper, a commented-out attempt, or a second redundant loop) do not cost the point.

Deduct only when one of the two methods is never invoked at all, when the needed values are taken by direct instance-variable (field) access on the record rather than by invoking the accessors, or when a method is applied to a receiver that is not a `CourseRecord` object (e.g., called on the list itself or on an ID/int value).
4:
**Sub-item 4 — Initializes count and increments it within a conditional statement (in the context of a loop)**

Award the point only when the response both declares/initializes a counter variable before the loop (or otherwise outside any loop that would reset it) and increments that counter by a statement that physically appears inside the body of a conditional statement — an `if`, `else`, `else if`, or `switch` case — that is itself inside a loop. The initialization may be incorrect (e.g., a wrong starting value), the response may fail to identify all the necessary students, may return early, and may call `getStudentID`/`getAbsences` incorrectly or not at all; none of that affects this point.

Deduct if the count is never initialized, or if it is initialized/reset inside a loop so that it restarts on each iteration. Also deduct whenever the increment statement is not contained in the body of an `if`/`else`/`else if`/`switch` case within a loop — including an unconditional increment, a guard-and-continue pattern (e.g., `if (...) continue;` followed by a bare `count++;`), ternary-expression counting (e.g., `count += cond ? 1 : 0;`), and boolean short-circuit tricks (e.g., `cond && count++ > 0;` or `count += cond ? ...` style expressions) — because in those cases the increment statement itself is not inside a conditional statement, even though its effect is conditional.
5:
**Sub-item 5 — Returns count of all and only necessary students (algorithm)**

Award the point when the response's algorithm counts exactly the students who meet the required condition and returns that count, and treat the student-ID match as correct whenever the IDs are compared using `.equals(...)` or any equivalent equals-based mechanism — for example a collection or map lookup (`contains`, `indexOf`, `get`, etc.) that performs its matching through `equals`. Such an ID match is semantically correct for Strings and is not a reason for deduction, regardless of the surface form it takes. Deduct only where the response uses `==` reference equality to compare the String IDs, or otherwise fails the item's stated requirements (e.g., fails to return the computed value, returns an incorrect value due to an early return, fails to compare all necessary pairs, fails to compare both IDs and absences, modifies either list, or prints the count instead of or in addition to returning it).
